content: Golfer's elbow, also known as medial epicondylitis, is an inflammatory condition affecting the elbow. It shares some similarities with tennis elbow but involves different anatomical structures. The condition primarily affects the flexor muscles of the forearm, which are responsible for bending the fingers and thumb, clenching the fist, and supinating the hand (excluding the biceps brachialis). These muscles converge into a common tendon that inserts into the medial epicondyle of the humerus at the elbow joint. In response to minor injuries or, in some cases, without any apparent cause, the insertion point of this tendon becomes inflamed. The term golfer's elbow arises because the tendon in question is stressed during a golf swing. However, many individuals who develop this condition have never played golf. It is also occasionally referred to as pitcher's elbow due to the similar stress placed on the tendon during the throwing of objects, such as a baseball, though this terminology is less commonly used. The primary symptom of golfer's elbow is pain localized to the medial aspect of the elbow joint. This pain is significantly exacerbated when the flexor muscles of the forearm are under tension but may also occur at rest. On physical examination, the medial epicondyle of the humerus is exquisitely tender to palpation. There may also be some weakness in the flexor muscles, which is attributed to pain-mediated reflex inhibition of their function. Treatment options include the use of simple analgesic medications and oral anti-inflammatory drugs. However, the definitive treatment involves the injection of a long-acting glucocorticoid (steroid) agent into and around the inflamed and tender area. While this injection may initially worsen symptoms for 24 to 48 hours, it typically leads to resolution of the condition within five to seven days. It is crucial to note that the ulnar nerve runs in the groove between the medial humeral epicondyle and the olecranon process of the ulna. Care must be taken to avoid accidental damage to this nerve during the administration of steroid injections for golfer's elbow.
